planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; candelabra tree is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere grown as a large container specimen.

directions: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; candelabra tree is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere grown as a large container specimen. Thick, angular, ribbed, spiny branches fork repeatedly upward in a dramatic candelabra pattern that gives this massive African succulent tree its common name, eventually reaching tree size in its native savanna habitat, where it provides an iconic, sculptural silhouette against the African sky. All parts contain a caustic, milky latex sap that severely irritates skin and eyes and is toxic if ingested, so handle with heavy gloves and eye protection during any pruning or propagation, and site away from children and pets. Water sparingly once established, provide maximum sun and heat, and grow young plants in a large container to move under cover for winter outside the warmest zones.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in lean, gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; Canary Island spurge is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere grown as a container specimen.

directions: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in lean, gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; Canary Island spurge is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere grown as a container specimen. Thick, deeply ribbed, spiny, cactus-like columns branch upward from the base into a dense, candelabra-shaped clump so convincingly cactus-like in appearance that it is often mistaken for a true cactus, despite being a completely unrelated succulent euphorbia from the volcanic slopes of the Canary Islands. All parts exude a caustic, irritating milky latex sap when cut or damaged, so handle with gloves and eye protection, and keep well away from children and pets. Water sparingly once established, provide maximum sun and sharp drainage, and grow young plants in a container to protect from any frost outside the warmest zones.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Medusa's Head euphorbia stores water in its thick central caudex and rots quickly in wet or dense soil.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Medusa's Head euphorbia stores water in its thick central caudex and rots quickly in wet or dense soil. Numerous thin, snaking, finger-like branches radiate outward from a swollen, partially buried central stem in a dramatic, writhing pattern that closely resembles the mythological gorgon's serpentine hair, tipped with small yellow-green flower clusters at each branch end. Native to South Africa's Eastern Cape, its milky sap is caustic and irritating like other euphorbias, so handle with gloves during any pruning or handling, keeping cut ends away from eyes and skin. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright light for the most compact, well-colored growth, and protect from any frost.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; African milk barrel needs excellent drainage and full sun to develop its best form and spine color.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; African milk barrel needs excellent drainage and full sun to develop its best form and spine color. Thick, ribbed, barrel-shaped, blue-gray stems armed with formidable dark spines closely resemble a true barrel cactus despite being an entirely unrelated South African euphorbia, slowly clustering into a small cluster of columnar stems over years of growth. All parts exude a caustic, irritating milky latex sap when cut, so handle with gloves and eye protection during any pruning or repotting, and keep well away from children and pets. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright light for compact, well-spined growth, and protect from any frost.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; mountain aloe is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere grown as a large container specimen.

directions: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; mountain aloe is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere grown as a large container specimen. Massive, thick, blue-gray leaves armed with reddish-brown thorns along the margins and scattered across both leaf surfaces form an enormous, single-trunked rosette that ranks among the largest and most architecturally imposing of all cultivated aloe species, topped in winter by branching flower spikes bearing dense clusters of orange to red tubular flowers. Native to rocky hillsides and savanna across southern Africa, it is a slow-growing but ultimately massive specimen well suited to a large-scale xeriscape or succulent garden where its bold, spiny form can be a focal point. Water only occasionally once established, provide full sun and excellent drainage, and give it ample room to eventually develop its substantial mature size.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; fan aloe needs excellent drainage and is one of the more distinctively shaped aloes, developing a branching, tree-like form.

directions: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; fan aloe needs excellent drainage and is one of the more distinctively shaped aloes, developing a branching, tree-like form. Flat, gray-green leaves arrange themselves in two neat, opposite ranks along each branch tip, forming a striking, hand-fan-shaped rosette unlike the typical spiral leaf arrangement of most other aloes, on a slow-growing, branching, shrub-to-small-tree form topped with orange-red flower spikes in late winter. Native to a very limited range in South Africa's Western Cape mountains, it is a highly prized specimen among aloe collectors for its unique fan-shaped growth habit and slow, tree-like branching structure that takes many years to develop. Water only occasionally once established, provide bright light with some protection from the most intense afternoon sun, and be patient with its slow, architecturally rewarding growth.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; soap aloe is one of the more cold-tolerant and adaptable aloe species, spreading readily by offsets into a dense colony.

directions: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; soap aloe is one of the more cold-tolerant and adaptable aloe species, spreading readily by offsets into a dense colony. Broad, spotted, blue-green leaves marked with irregular white blotches form a dense rosette that offsets freely into a spreading colony, topped by branching spikes of coral-orange to red flowers over an unusually long season, and the leaf sap has traditionally been used across southern Africa as a soap substitute, giving the species its common name. One of the toughest and most adaptable aloe species in cultivation, it tolerates more cold, drought, and neglect than many other aloes, spreading steadily by offsets to form an increasingly showy colony over time. Water only occasionally once established, and divide congested clumps to propagate or control spread as needed.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Golden Tooth aloe offsets readily and develops its best coppery-orange color in bright, direct light.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Golden Tooth aloe offsets readily and develops its best coppery-orange color in bright, direct light. Thick, triangular leaves edged with small, bright golden-yellow teeth form a dense, symmetrical rosette that flushes warm coppery-orange to bronze in bright, stressed light, offsetting freely at the base to form an attractive clustering mound, and mature plants send up tall spikes of red-orange, tubular flowers. Its compact size, freely offsetting habit, and striking bronze coloring in strong light make it a popular, easy aloe for a sunny windowsill collection or xeriscape container garden. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide as much bright direct light as possible for the richest color, and separate offsets to propagate or share.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference
